1.pericope_label: Then he brought me forth into the utter court, the way toward the north: and he brought me into the chamber that was over against the separate place, and which was before the building toward the north. Before the length of an hundred cubits was the north door, and the breadth was fifty cubits. Over against the twenty cubits which were for the inner court, and over against the pavement which was for the utter court, was gallery against gallery in three stories. And before the chambers was a walk of ten cubits breadth inward, a way of one cubit; and their doors toward the north. Now the upper chambers were shorter: for the galleries were higher than these, than the lower, and than the middlemost of the building. For they were in three stories, but had not pillars as the pillars of the courts: therefore the building was straitened more than the lowest and the middlemost from the ground. And the wall that was without over against the chambers, toward the utter court on the forepart of the chambers, the length thereof was fifty cubits. For the length of the chambers that were in the utter court was fifty cubits: and, lo, before the temple were an hundred cubits. And from under these chambers was the entry on the east side, as one goeth into them from the utter court.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch call the structure a cell-building and take apart the reading that makes the disputed way of one cubit the width of the entrances, on three grounds — the word is used collectively after one that is not and before a plural noun for their doors, a way is not the same thing as an entrance or a doorway, and an opening of a single cubit into a large building would bear no proportion to a walk of ten cubits — concluding that no suitable meaning can be got from the words as they stand; Ellicott keeps the plain sense of outer for the court, works out that the building must have run the whole remaining length west of the separate place since a later passage shows it did not reach the western wall, argues from the northern door that the entrance lay necessarily in the outer court and that the long axis ran east and west, notes that the measurements are external because the prophet never entered, calls the gallery phrase difficult since the word rendered against is literally unto the face of and the word for storeys is missing, proposes a gallery in the third storey of each block set on the facing sides, emends the way of one cubit to a hundred on the authority of the Greek and of a parallel transposition corrected in the Hebrew margin later in the chapter, and identifies the screen-wall by its distinct vocabulary as a fence at the eastern end shielding the priests as they changed their garments.

Gill has the prophet led out into the surrounding court on the north side after the house itself has been described, takes the three storeys as set one above another with the middle shorter than the lowest and the top shorter still, and reads the screen-wall as the grace that separates and protects the churches.

Clarke takes the move to be out of the temple into the priests' court, which he says is called the outer court only relative to the temple, the people's court lying further out still; Wesley sets the house itself on the southern prospect of the chambers, divides the galleries so that one faces the inner court and another the pavement with the chambers between, insists that the shortening of the upper chambers refers to height rather than length, and keeps the disputed cubit as a ledge running along the building, called a way though nobody was meant to walk on it.

Henry reads the whole block morally: private rooms stand about the place of public worship because attendance on the ordinances excuses nobody from the closet, they stand within sight of the house because private devotion prepares for public rather than replacing it, and the walk before them is where those lodging there met and talked for mutual edification.

debates.question: Which court is the prophet brought out into?

positions.position: The court surrounding the house on the north, entered from the north gate.
The priests' court, which is called the outer court only in relation to the temple, the people's court lying beyond it.
The outer court in the plain sense, and the prophet is brought to the building rather than into it.

debates.question: What is meant by a way of one cubit?

positions.position: Nothing intelligible as the text stands: the entrance reading fails on grammar, on vocabulary, and on proportion alike.

The text is corrupt: read a hundred with the Greek, a change of one transposition and one letter, giving a walk that reaches exactly to the steps of the inner north gate where the sacrifices were dressed.
A ledge one cubit wide running along the building, called a way although nobody was meant to walk on it.

outliers.claim: Turns the architecture into a rule for devotion, since chambers set about the place of public worship show that neither the closet nor the assembly may be dropped for the other.
Notices that the remark about pillars, made to prove the galleries had no external support, incidentally discloses that the courts had pillars at all, most likely cloisters as in the later temple.

10.pericope_label: The chambers were in the thickness of the wall of the court toward the east, over against the separate place, and over against the building. And the way before them was like the appearance of the chambers which were toward the north, as long as they, and as broad as they: and all their goings out were both according to their fashions, and according to their doors. And according to the doors of the chambers that were toward the south was a door in the head of the way, even the way directly before the wall toward the east, as one entereth into them. Then said he unto me, The north chambers and the south chambers, which are before the separate place, they be holy chambers, where the priests that approach unto the Lord shall eat the most holy things: there shall they lay the most holy things, and the meat offering, and the sin offering, and the trespass offering; for the place is holy. When the priests enter therein, then shall they not go out of the holy place into the utter court, but there they shall lay their garments wherein they minister; for they are holy; and shall put on other garments, and shall approach to those things which are for the people. Now when he had made an end of measuring the inner house, he brought me forth toward the gate whose prospect is toward the east, and measured it round about. He measured the east side with the measuring reed, five hundred reeds, with the measuring reed round about. He measured the north side, five hundred reeds, with the measuring reed round about. He measured the south side, five hundred reeds, with the measuring reed. He turned about to the west side, and measured five hundred reeds with the measuring reed. He measured it by the four sides: it had a wall round about, five hundred reeds long, and five hundred broad, to make a separation between the sanctuary and the profane place.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch record that the extent of the measured area has divided opinion since ancient times; Ellicott renders the eastern block as matching the northern in length, breadth, exits and doors, warns that the following verse contains a word found nowhere else in the language, identifies its wall with the screen already described so that the path from the gate porch met the passage at right angles, admits that these chambers have no counterpart in the older building to guide an interpreter, refers both clauses about the holy things to the priests' portion and argues that uncooked flesh cannot have been laid where the eating was done since the boiling happened elsewhere, notices that peace offerings go unmentioned because the law never required them to be eaten in a holy place, reaches the rule about the garments cautiously since the law only implies it, makes the arithmetic of the precinct explicit at six cubits to the rod and five hundred rods to the side, holds the rod decisive against attempts to shrink the enclosure, and concludes with Keil that the temple was never meant to stand in the old city or anywhere on earth, the vision not being designed for material realisation.

Gill notes that chambers stood on the eastern side as well as the north and south, has the measuring begin at the east and take four equal sides in turn, and concludes from the scale that no material building can be meant, since no such edifice ever stood, so that the enormous square must signify the largeness of the church in the latter day.

Clarke states the rule about the vestments flatly, that they were for ministry only, might not be worn in the outer court, and were left in these chambers when the service ended, says it is no wonder the place was called a city, describes what the separating wall excluded, since no stranger or unclean person might enter the consecrated ground while the outer space admitted anyone, and cites the historian for a low barrier standing in his own day with notices in two languages forbidding foreigners to pass on pain of death; Wesley makes some of the chambers a store-house for what was not in present use, and repeats Henry's reading of the great square almost word for word, though his circuit runs to eight miles where Henry's runs to four.

Henry measures the sides at about an English mile and calls the whole the suburbs of a mystical temple, signifying how far the church would extend when all nations were discipled, fulfilled in part already and to be finished when the fulness of the Gentiles comes in, and draws the rule out of the surrounding wall that a difference is to be put between common and sacred things and a distance between worldly and religious actions, so that we come to worship with a solemn pause.

debates.question: How large was the measured precinct, and can it be a real site?

positions.position: Five hundred rods a side, the rod being six cubits, so about a mile each way; the rod is decisive against attempts to shrink it, and no earthly locality was intended.
The extent has been disputed since ancient times, the Greek translators and a line of modern scholars reading the figure differently.
The area is so vast that it is no wonder the place is called a city.
No material building can be meant at all, since no edifice of such dimensions ever stood.

debates.question: What does the size of the enclosure signify?

positions.position: The suburbs of a mystical temple, marking how far the church would reach when all nations were discipled, fulfilled in part and to be completed when the fulness of the Gentiles comes in.
The largeness of the church in the latter day, when the Jews are converted and the Gentiles brought in.
That the vision was never designed for material realisation anywhere on earth.

outliers.claim: Reaches outside the text for the historian's account of a low barrier standing in his own day, carrying notices in two languages that forbade foreigners to pass it on pain of death.
Admits that these chambers, unlike the rest of the vision, have no counterpart in the older building to guide an interpreter, and suspects an unmentioned second entrance for the priests.
